subject: 중세 유럽의 시계와 노동 시간
title: Clocks and the medieval working day
content: Before mechanical clocks, the medieval day was divided by tasks and by the sun, so an hour in summer was longer than an hour in winter and nobody found this odd. Work began at first light and ended when the light failed, and the bells that marked the day rang for prayer rather than for labour. What changed when town clocks appeared was not merely accuracy but the unit itself, since a mechanical escapement divides the day into equal parts regardless of the season. The new hours were adopted first where they were useful to someone. Cloth towns installed clocks whose bells signalled the start and end of work, and the disputes that followed show what was at stake, because employers and weavers disagreed about who controlled the bell. Records survive of workers destroying a clock and of ordinances forbidding its adjustment, and both indicate that the instrument had become a party to the bargain rather than a neutral measure. Its spread therefore tracked commerce rather than science. Monasteries had kept mechanical time earlier without any of these consequences, since their day was already fixed by rule, and the towns that adopted clocks were those where labour was hired by the day and where the length of that day was contested. Historians accordingly read the medieval clock as an instrument of the wage relation as much as of timekeeping.

subject: 중세 대학의 성립과 이동
title: How medieval universities formed and moved
content: A medieval university began not as a building but as a sworn association, and this fact explains much of what it could do. Masters and students bound themselves by oath, and the resulting corporation could negotiate with the town, set its own admission standards, and discipline its members. Because the association was the university, it could pick up and leave, and several of the great foundations began when a body of scholars walked out of one town and settled in another. Departure was the strongest instrument they had. A town that hosted scholars gained rents, food sales, and prestige, so the threat of removal gave the corporation leverage in disputes over prices, over the jurisdiction of courts, and over the punishment of members. The records of these quarrels are full of appeals to distant authorities, since a body with no walls needed a protector, and popes and kings granted privileges that the towns then had to honour. What followed was a peculiar kind of independence. The medieval university owed its freedoms to outside patrons rather than to any local right, and those freedoms lasted as long as the patrons found them useful. Historians therefore treat the mobility of early universities as the mechanism that produced their autonomy, since an institution that cannot leave has far less to bargain with.

subject: 중세 아이슬란드의 법과 분쟁 해결
title: Law and feud in medieval Iceland
content: Medieval Iceland had courts, an assembly, and an elaborate body of law, and yet it had no king, no police, and no officer charged with enforcing a verdict. A successful plaintiff who won his case had to collect the judgment himself, with whatever support his kin and allies would provide, and this arrangement shaped everything about how disputes proceeded. Litigation was therefore inseparable from the balance of force. What made the system work at all was that support could be bought and traded. A man with a strong claim but few allies could transfer his case to someone powerful enough to press it, and the sagas record such transfers constantly, which means that legal rights functioned as assets with a market. Chieftains accumulated cases as they accumulated followers, and their standing rested on both. The result was neither anarchy nor the rule of law as later centuries understood it. Violence was constrained by the requirement that it be justified in legal terms afterward, and a killing that could not be defended at the assembly cost its author dearly in support. Historians therefore read the medieval Icelandic evidence as showing how far law can operate without enforcement, and also where the limit lies, since the system finally broke when a few families grew large enough that no coalition could check them.

subject: 고대 로마의 곡물 수입과 항구
title: Grain imports and the harbours of ancient Rome
content: An ancient city of a million people cannot be fed from its own countryside, and Rome solved this by importing grain across the sea from provinces that produced a surplus. The scale of the operation shaped the whole Mediterranean, because the ships, harbours, warehouses, and officials required to move that quantity every year formed a system with no earlier parallel. Its remains are among the most substantial the ancient world left. Harbour construction shows the difficulty most clearly. The natural mouth of the river silted and could not take large vessels, so successive emperors built artificial basins with moles reaching into open water, and the excavated plans show warehouses arranged for rapid unloading. Because the sailing season was short and the city held only a few months of reserve, delays in one season produced shortage in the next, and the ancient sources record riots when the fleet was late. Responsibility for the supply therefore became political. An official charged with the grain held one of the most important posts in the administration, and emperors advertised their care of the supply on coins and in inscriptions. Historians read the harbours and warehouses as evidence that feeding the ancient capital was a permanent state undertaking rather than a matter left to merchants.

subject: 고대 중국의 철 국영과 재정
title: State iron and revenue in ancient China
content: An ancient Chinese administration took iron and salt production into state hands, and the debate that followed survives in a text preserving both sides. Officials defending this policy pointed to the revenue it raised without taxing farmers directly, and they pointed to the value of controlling the metal from which ancient weapons were made. Their opponents argued that state workshops turned out tools poorly suited to real farming, and that prices rose once competition had been removed. What this debate reveals is a genuine problem of ancient administration rather than a simple contest of interests. Iron was both a military necessity and an agricultural one, so a policy tuned to the first could damage the second. The complaints recorded about implement quality are specific enough to be credible, since a plough made to one standard pattern will not suit every soil, and local variation had been the strength of the private workshops this monopoly displaced. The policy was relaxed and reimposed several times over the following centuries, which indicates that neither side had settled the question. Historians treat the surviving debate as unusually valuable, because ancient sources rarely preserve arguments against a policy in the words of those who made them, and here those objections are stated fully enough to be weighed.

subject: 증언은 왜 지식의 원천인가
title: Why testimony counts as knowledge
content: Almost everything a person believes was learned from someone else, and yet philosophy long treated testimony as a second-rate source, acceptable only where it could in principle be checked by observation or argument. That view is difficult to sustain once its consequences are traced, because nobody has checked the history, geography, or science she takes for granted, and demanding that she do so would leave her knowing almost nothing. Two positions now compete. One holds that testimony is credible by default, so a hearer is entitled to believe what she is told unless she has some specific reason for doubt. This matches how people actually reason and explains how knowledge accumulates across a community. Critics answer that it licenses gullibility and that trust ought to be earned by evidence of reliability. The rival position requires such evidence, holding that a hearer needs grounds for thinking her source trustworthy before belief is warranted. Its difficulty is that those grounds must themselves come largely from testimony, so the requirement threatens a regress. Most current accounts accept default trust while insisting that it is defeasible, and the interesting work concerns what defeats it. Signals about how a claim was produced, whether the speaker has an interest in it, and whether independent sources converge all bear on the question, and none of them requires checking the claim directly.

subject: 고대 이집트의 나일 범람 측정
title: Measuring the ancient flood of the Nile
content: The annual flood of the Nile determined how much land could be sown, so an ancient administration that knew its height in advance could estimate the harvest before it was planted. Structures built to measure that height survive at several points along the river, cut as staircases descending into the water with marks recording each level. Readings taken at the southern stations reached the ancient capital before the flood itself did, and this gave its officials weeks of warning. What these measurements supported was assessment rather than farming. A high flood meant a large sown area and a large expected yield, and dues were set accordingly, so the readings translated into projections that scribes could work from. Records of such levels were kept over long periods, and the surviving series is among the longest environmental datasets the ancient world left, which modern climatologists have since used for purposes its compilers never imagined. The system also carried a political charge. A ruler under whom the flood came well was credited with that outcome, and a run of poor floods weakened claims resting on divine favour. Ancient texts accordingly record these levels alongside reigns, and historians read the pairing as evidence that the measurement was never a purely technical exercise.

subject: 운과 책임의 경계
title: Where luck ends and responsibility begins
content: We hold people responsible for what they do and excuse them for what merely happens to them, and this distinction seems clear until we ask where it falls. A driver who kills a pedestrian through carelessness is blamed far more than one equally careless who arrives home safely, though the difference lies entirely in what neither controlled. Moral philosophy calls this moral luck, and it exposes a conflict between two things we firmly believe. The first is that blame should track control, since holding someone responsible for what she could not affect seems plainly unfair. The second is that outcomes matter, and our practices of blame, punishment, and compensation are built around them everywhere. Attempts to keep both have not succeeded, because any principle strong enough to secure the first denies the second, and any concession to the second abandons the first. The dispute extends further than driving cases. Whether a person is generous depends partly on whether she was raised among generous people, and whether she faces a moral test at all depends on circumstances she did not arrange. Once these are admitted, control shrinks toward vanishing, and some philosophers conclude that responsibility as we ordinarily understand it cannot be defended. Others hold that the ordinary practice is sound and that the demand for control was always too strict.

subject: 권위에 복종할 의무가 있는가
title: Whether we must obey authority
content: Most people accept that they ought to obey the law, and political philosophy has found it surprisingly hard to say why. The obvious answers turn out to justify something narrower than what they were meant to support, because they give reasons to do what the law happens to require rather than reasons to obey it as law. If a statute forbids assault, the wrong of assault already supplies the reason, and the statute adds nothing. Consent is the traditional answer, and it fails on the facts, since almost nobody has agreed to anything and residence is a poor substitute for agreement when leaving is not realistic. Appeals to benefit fare a little better, holding that one who accepts the goods a legal order provides owes compliance in return, and yet benefits that arrive unasked do not usually create debts. Appeals to coordination explain traffic rules well and explain very little else. What follows if no general obligation exists is less alarming than it sounds. A person may still have strong reasons to comply in most cases, arising from the harm disobedience would cause, the value of stable institutions, and fairness to others who comply. What she lacks is a further reason grounded in authority itself, and philosophers who accept this conclusion argue that political obligation was always doing less work than its defenders supposed.

subject: 동남아시아의 향료 재배와 항구 국가
title: Spice growing and the port states of Southeast Asia
content: Cloves and nutmeg grew on a small number of islands and nowhere else, and this accident of botany shaped the politics of a whole region for centuries. The islands themselves were modest in population and produced little else, yet the demand for what they grew drew shipping from across the ocean and made the waters around them worth controlling. Power accordingly settled not on the growing islands but on the ports that commanded the routes to them. Such a port state had a characteristic form. It held little territory, drew its revenue from duties on passing trade, and maintained its position by offering shelter, warehouses, and a ruler who would enforce bargains among merchants of many origins. Its strength depended on remaining the convenient place to stop, so a rival that offered lower duties or better security could draw the traffic away within a few seasons. The historical record shows several such shifts. What made these states fragile also made them tolerant, since a port that excluded a community of traders lost their business to a competitor. Multiple languages, laws, and religions therefore coexisted in them as a condition of prosperity rather than as a policy. Historians read this pattern as the consequence of an economy built on transit, and the same pattern appears wherever a state lives on traffic it does not produce.

subject: 표현의 자유와 해악의 거리
title: Free expression and the distance to harm
content: Defenders of free expression rarely claim that speech never causes damage, and the interesting moral question is how close the connection must be before restriction becomes legitimate. Words that directly incite an immediate attack are treated differently from words that gradually shift what an audience finds acceptable, and this difference is one of distance between the utterance and the injury. Where that distance is short, causation is clear and the case for restriction is strong. The difficulty arises with longer chains. Speech that degrades a group may make violence against it more likely without any particular utterance producing any particular assault, so the harm is real while its causal path runs through the free choices of many people. Some philosophers argue that these intervening choices break responsibility, so the speaker cannot be held to account for what others decided to do. Others reply that this ignores how moral attitudes are formed, and that it treats each choice as though it were made in a vacuum. The practical stakes are considerable, because the answer decides whether a legal order may act before harm occurs or only afterward. Most positions accept that some restriction is warranted while insisting that the threshold be high and its rules be clear, since vague standards chill far more speech than they were written to reach.

subject: 고대의 유리 제조와 전파
title: Ancient glassmaking and how it spread
content: Ancient glass was made from sand, plant ash, and lime, and the earliest workshops produced small vessels by winding molten threads around a clay core that was scraped out once the glass had cooled. This method was slow and its products were costly, so glass in that period served the purposes of precious stone and travelled in the same circles. Everything changed when someone discovered that a gather of molten glass could be inflated with a blowpipe. Blowing made vessels quickly and thinly, and it needed far less raw material for a given volume, so the price of a cup fell within a generation from something a wealthy ancient household would display to something an ordinary one would use. The archaeological record registers this shift sharply, since glass appears in contexts where it had never occurred before. Few ancient technologies changed their social distribution so fast. What spread with the technique was a division of labour. Raw glass continued to be made where the right sand lay, and it was shipped in slabs to workshops that reheated and blew it wherever customers were, so making and forming became separate ancient trades in separate regions. Historians trace this arrangement through chemical analysis, because the composition of a finished vessel identifies the distant source of its raw material.
